title: A Room for the Cellar
premise: Late-night radio host Theo Quintana begins receiving calls from listeners who died the previous week, and his own sleep recordings reveal a second voice answering questions he never asked aloud. The voice belongs to something invited into the house decades ago by his grandmother — a bargain sealed with a well beneath the cellar that refills every generation. As Theo's dead callers guide him toward the truth, his partner Marisol must choose between loyalty to him and the duty her own family owes the thing below. Theo survives to sunrise only by speaking the invitation aloud and refusing it, breaking the cycle at the cost of the station, the house, and the version of himself that kept the lights on.
about_author: Theo Pemberton is a former overnight radio producer from coastal Maine who spent six years answering a small-town call-in line before turning those sleepless hours into fiction. 'A Room for the Cellar' is his second novel, written in the hours between sign-off and sunrise.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. During his 2 a.m. show, a caller describes her own funeral from last Tuesday; Theo assumes a prank until three more dead listeners phone in, each asking him to keep the lights on. The beat is quiet dread — the professional mask holding while the world tilts.

chapters.title: The Counted Doors
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. He walks the house counting doors — eleven inside, twelve on the recording of his footsteps. He tells no one, including Marisol, choosing routine over confession. Emotional beat: denial dressed as competence.

chapters.title: Sleep Study
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. A sound engineer friend gives Theo a recorder for his insomnia; Marisol listens back and hears a second voice answering questions Theo never asked. She hides the tape, torn between protecting him and protecting herself. Beat: love against self-preservation.

chapters.title: Caller Number Seven
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. A dead caller names Theo's grandmother and says, 'Ask her what she promised.' Theo digs out her effects and finds a ledger of names, each crossed out on a date matching a local death. Beat: curiosity outrunning fear.

chapters.title: What Marisol Kept
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol plays Theo the tape; the second voice says his name in his grandmother's cadence. They fight — she accuses him of hiding the calls, he accuses her of listening in secret. Beat: intimacy cracking under shared fear.

chapters.title: The Well Beneath
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. In the cellar he finds a bricked alcove behind shelving, warm to the touch, humming like a held breath. The dead callers go silent when he stands before it. Beat: awe curdling into violation.

chapters.title: Duty of the Delgados
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol's mother arrives unannounced, recognizes the house instantly, and reveals the Delgado family has served as 'doorkeepers' for generations — feeding the thing names so it never takes their own. Beat: loyalty revealed as complicity.

chapters.title: Refill
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The well 'refills': every light in town flickers, and the dead callers return changed, reciting the ledger aloud on air. Listeners hear it live. Theo keeps broadcasting because stopping feels like opening a door. Beat: performance as survival.

chapters.title: Names Given Freely
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol learns her mother gave the thing Theo's name years ago as insurance. Confrontation in the kitchen: duty versus love made explicit. Marisol burns her copy of the family page. Beat: betrayal and choice.

chapters.title: The Second Voice Explains
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. During sleep, Theo finally asks the voice questions directly. It answers patiently: it was invited, it keeps its bargains, and it has never once opened a door that wasn't offered. Beat: horror through reasonableness.

chapters.title: Interference
chapters.summary: Station engineer Dev's POV. Dev notices the broadcast signal originating partly from inside Theo's house, not the tower. He drives over, hears the show airing with no one at the microphone, and flees. Beat: external witness confirms the impossible.

chapters.title: Sunrise Deadline
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The dead callers, briefly themselves again, warn him: the well refills fully at dawn, and whatever name sits uncrossed in the ledger then is claimed. His name is next. Beat: clock started, dread sharpened to purpose.

chapters.title: What Was Invited
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol deciphers the ledger's first page: her great-grandmother and Theo's grandmother jointly invited the thing during the flood of 1954, trading a room in every descendant's house for the town's survival. Beat: history reframed as shared guilt.

chapters.title: Doors Twelve Through One
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The house rearranges overnight; doors lead into other doorkeepers' homes across town, all standing open, all dark. Theo walks them, closing each, feeling the thing watch without malice. Beat: loneliness at scale.

chapters.title: The Call-In Confession
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo goes on air and confesses everything — the calls, the ledger, the well. Half the town thinks it's a stunt; a handful call in whispering that they've heard the second voice too. Beat: truth as weapon and exposure.

chapters.title: Mother's Bargain
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol's mother offers the thing a substitute name — Marisol's — to protect the family line. Marisol finds the fresh ink drying in the ledger. Beat: duty's cruelty fully revealed.

chapters.title: Crossed Out
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo crosses out his own name preemptively; the house retaliates, sealing him in the cellar with the warm alcove as the walls begin breathing in earnest. Beat: defiance met with pressure.

chapters.title: What Marisol Owes
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol descends against her mother's orders, using the doorkeeper's words her mother taught her — not to banish, but to negotiate. She offers the thing what it actually wants: to be released from the bargain rather than fed. Beat: love weaponized as courage.

chapters.title: The Invitation Spoken
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Together they speak the original invitation aloud, word for word from the ledger, and then both refuse it. The thing cannot stay where it is not welcomed; the alcove cracks; the dead callers say goodbye one by one on air. Beat: climax — ritual, refusal, release.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Dawn comes with the well dry and the twelfth door gone. The station's transmitter burns out mid-sign-off, ending the show forever. Theo weeps with relief and grief in equal measure. Beat: exhaustion after survival.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Weeks later: the house sold, Marisol estranged from her mother but certain, Dev rebuilding the station as a podcast, the ledger burned except the first page, which they keep as testimony. Beat: cost acknowledged, bond affirmed.

chapters.title: A Room, Empty
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, epilogue. Theo records one final solo episode from a rented room: no calls come, and for the first time silence sounds like silence. Then, faintly, a knock — and he chooses not to answer. Beat: peace chosen daily, horror honored but closed.
